attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	
6	\paragraph{Model and Predictor.}
7	We evaluate on LLaMA-3.1-8B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama3}, which uses SwiGLU FFN blocks~\cite{shazeer2020glu} with $d_{\text{model}}=4096$ and $d_{\text{ff}}=14336$ across 32 layers.
8	The sparsity predictor is a two-layer MLP with 2.37M parameters per layer (75.9M total), implemented as Linear($4096 \to 128$) + GELU + Linear($128 \to 14336$), trained to produce per-neuron importance scores that minimize output-distribution divergence under sparsity.
9	
10	\paragraph{Training.}
11	All predictors are trained for 1000 steps on WikiText-103 with sequence length 2048 and batch size 4, using AdamW~\cite{loshchilov2019adamw} with learning rate $1 \times 10^{-3}$, weight decay $5 \times 10^{-2}$, and cosine decay.
12	The KL predictor uses Gumbel-Sigmoid relaxation~\cite{jang2017gumbel} with temperature $\tau=1.0$ annealed to $0.1$ over training.
13	
14	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
15	We report perplexity on WikiText-2~\cite{merity2017pointer} (seq\_len=2048) and downstream accuracy on ARC-Challenge (25-shot), WinoGrande (5-shot), MMLU (5-shot), and GSM8K (8-shot).
16	
17	\paragraph{Inference Protocol.}
18	At inference, the predictor produces per-neuron scores that are passed to TEAL's global top-$k$ allocation mechanism~\cite{liu2025teal}, which distributes the sparsity budget across layers non-uniformly.
19	We term this \textit{predictor-TEAL}: the predictor replaces TEAL's magnitude-based scoring while retaining its allocation strategy.
20	
21	\paragraph{Baselines.}
22	We compare against: (1) \textbf{Vanilla TEAL}~\cite{liu2025teal}, which uses activation magnitudes directly; (2) \textbf{BCE predictor} (DejaVu-style~\cite{liu2023dejavu}), trained with per-neuron binary cross-entropy on magnitude-based oracle masks for 1000 and 2700 steps; (3) \textbf{Uniform allocation}, which distributes the sparsity budget equally across layers; and (4) \textbf{WINA}~\cite{liu2025teal}, an importance-weighted variant.
23	
24	
25	\subsection{Main Results}
26	
27	Table~\ref{tab:main} presents the primary comparison. We recommend uniform allocation for deployment (best downstream preservation); global allocation is analyzed to understand allocation-quality tradeoffs (\S\ref{sec:scaling}).
28	At 30\% sparsity, KL distillation with global TEAL allocation achieves PPL 8.98, reducing TEAL's degradation from dense (10.97 $\to$ 8.98, an 18\% improvement). % exp_id: kl_30_global_teal
29	Uniform allocation at 30\% provides stable downstream performance (MMLU 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed) while global top-$k$ exhibits high seed variance (35.7$\pm$9.5\%), with late-layer starvation (L31 retention 28.4\%) interacting with predictor initialization (\S\ref{sec:scaling}). % exp_id: bench_kl30_uniform, kl30_3seed
30	
31	At 50\% sparsity, KL distillation over vanilla TEAL widens the PPL advantage: 11.79 vs.\ 23.31, a 49\% reduction. % exp_id: bench_kl50_global, bench_teal50
32	The predictor also generalizes to held-out data (C4 validation: 52.5\% advantage over TEAL; see Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
33	However, all methods exhibit downstream collapse on MMLU (28.1$\pm$0.2\% vs.\ 28.0$\pm$0.6\%, both $\approx$ random, 3-seed) and GSM8K ($<$2.2\%), indicating a capacity-limited regime where no allocation strategy can recover. % exp_id: bench_kl50_global, d030_kl50_uniform, multi_seed_kl50_global
34	
35	\begin{table}[t]
36	\centering
37	\caption{Main results on LLaMA-3.1-8B. PPL$\downarrow$ on WikiText-2; accuracy$\uparrow$ on downstream tasks. \textbf{Bold}: best among compensation-free methods per sparsity level. BCE follows the DejaVu~\cite{liu2023dejavu} predictor pipeline (per-neuron BCE on magnitude oracles) with a FastForward-style~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} compensation network (67.2M params) applied post-masking; no TEAL allocation. KL MMLU at 30\% and 50\% reports 3-seed mean$\pm$std; 50\% uniform PPL is 3-seed ($11.92 \pm 0.07$; Appendix~\ref{app:stability}); all other entries use seed 42.}
38	\label{tab:main}
39	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
40	\begin{tabular}{llccccc}
41	\toprule
42	Sparsity & Method & PPL$\downarrow$ & ARC-c & WG & MMLU & GSM8K \\
43	\midrule
44	0\% & Dense & 6.12 & 58.28 & 78.06 & 65.27 & 48.75 \\
45	\midrule
46	\multirow{3}{*}{30\%}
47	& TEAL vanilla & 10.97 & \textbf{42.32} & 66.06 & 38.61 & 7.88 \\ % exp_id: bench_teal30
48	& KL global (Ours) & 8.98 & 39.68 & \textbf{70.17} & 35.7$\pm$9.5 & \textbf{8.79} \\ % exp_id: kl30_3seed_global
49	& KL uniform & \textbf{8.82} & 40.78 & 68.59 & \textbf{40.7$\pm$1.3} & 7.35 \\ % exp_id: kl30_3seed_uniform
50	\midrule
51	\multirow{4}{*}{50\%}
52	& TEAL vanilla & 23.31 & 28.41 & 53.04 & \textbf{28.32} & 1.97 \\ % exp_id: bench_teal50
53	& KL global (Ours) & \textbf{11.79} & \textbf{32.85} & \textbf{63.46} & 28.1$\pm$0.2 & 1.29 \\ % exp_id: multi_seed_kl50_global
54	& KL uniform & 11.96 & 32.76 & 62.90 & 28.0$\pm$0.6 & \textbf{2.12} \\ % exp_id: multi_seed_kl50_uniform
55	& BCE (2700 steps)$^\ast$ & 27.97 & 23.98 & 50.59 & 30.02 & 4.85 \\ % exp_id: eval_bce_v3_s42
56	\bottomrule
57	\end{tabular}}
58	\end{table}
59	
60	
61	\subsection{Extended Training Analysis}
62	\label{sec:isocompute}
63	
64	To test whether BCE simply requires more compute, we train it for 2700 steps (2.71$\times$ the KL step budget, approximately equal wall-clock time: $\sim$46 min BCE vs.\ $\sim$45 min KL on RTX PRO 6000).
65	The BCE predictor achieves PPL 27.97, still 2.37$\times$ worse than KL at 1000 steps (PPL 11.79). % exp_id: bce_isocompute_s42
66	The failure is structural, not due to architectural or compute differences: both predictors use identical architectures and TEAL allocation, yet BCE achieves +7pp oracle F1 (0.613 vs.\ 0.540) with 137\% worse PPL (27.97 vs.\ 11.79). KL's near-random precision (0.51) confirms it learns a mask optimized for distributional fidelity rather than magnitude matching. % exp_id: f1_oracle_analysis, bce_isocompute_s42
67	Future work could further isolate coupling effects through MSE on hidden states and per-layer KL ablations.
68	
69	
70	\subsection{Ablation Studies}
71	
72	Table~\ref{tab:ablation} isolates the contribution of each design choice at 50\% sparsity.
73	
74	\begin{table}[t]
75	\centering
76	\caption{Ablation at 50\% sparsity on LLaMA-3.1-8B (WikiText-2 PPL$\downarrow$, unified benchmark protocol).}
77	\label{tab:ablation}
78	\small
79	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
80	\toprule
81	Configuration & PPL$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$ from Ours \\
82	\midrule
83	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{KL-based variants}} \\
84	Forward KL + Gumbel (Ours) & \textbf{11.79} & --- \\ % exp_id: bench_kl50_global
85	JSD (symmetric) + Gumbel & 12.54 & +0.75 \\ % exp_id: jsd_ablation_s42
86	Reverse KL + Gumbel & 12.80 & +1.01 \\ % exp_id: reverse_kl_ablation_s42
87	Forward KL + STE & 15.77 & +3.98 \\ % exp_id: ste_baseline_s42
88	\midrule
89	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{BCE-based variants}} \\
90	BCE + Compensation (hard mask) & 25.44 & +13.65 \\ % exp_id: bce_comp_staged_s42
91	BCE (no compensation) & 27.97 & +16.18 \\ % exp_id: eval_bce_v3_s42
92	BCE + Gumbel + Penalty (no KL) & 38.02 & +26.23 \\ % exp_id: bce_gumbel_lagrangian_isolation
93	\bottomrule
94	\end{tabular}
95	\end{table}
96	
97	\paragraph{Gumbel vs.\ STE.}
98	Replacing Gumbel-Sigmoid with STE~\cite{bengio2013ste} degrades PPL from 11.79 to 15.77 (+3.98), accounting for 34.5\% of the improvement over vanilla TEAL. % exp_id: ste_baseline_s42
99	
100	\paragraph{Divergence Direction.}
101	Forward KL (mode-covering) outperforms JSD (+6.4\%) and reverse KL (+8.6\%), consistent with the SNR analysis in \S\ref{sec:method:gradient}: complete teacher supervision enables better global allocation learning. % exp_id: jsd_ablation_s42, reverse_kl_ablation_s42
102	This contrasts with MiniLLM~\cite{gu2024minillm}, which finds reverse KL superior for sequence-level distillation: in generation, mode-seeking prevents low-probability token production, while in mask prediction, mode-covering (forward KL) ensures no important neuron is omitted ($q(x) \approx 0$ where $p(x) > 0$ is directly penalized).
103	
104	\paragraph{SPON Contribution.}
105	Adding SPON~\cite{xu2026spon} bias correction reduces PPL from 12.08 to 11.79 (2.4\% relative); see \S\ref{sec:spon} for decomposition.\footnote{SPON analysis uses \texttt{evaluate.py}; main results use the unified benchmark.} % exp_id: spon_2048_s42, mvp_kl_norm_v2_s42
106	
107	\paragraph{Loss Function Isolation.}
108	BCE with identical Gumbel-Sigmoid and penalty yields PPL 38.02, worse than vanilla BCE (27.97): the penalty interferes with per-neuron optimization without global coordination. % exp_id: bce_gumbel_lagrangian_isolation
109	The loss effect ($\Delta$PPL=26.23) is $6.6\times$ the relaxation effect ($\Delta$PPL=3.98).
110	
111	\paragraph{BCE + Compensation.}
112	FastForward-style compensation~\cite{gautam2026fastforward} improves BCE from 27.97 to 25.44 (9.0\%), still $2.16\times$ worse than KL. % exp_id: bce_comp_staged_s42
113	
114	\paragraph{Hyperparameter Robustness.}
115	Appendix~\ref{app:db_sensitivity} confirms robustness to predictor capacity ($d_b$, $<$3\%), temperature ($<$1.8\%), and training steps (saturated by 800). % exp_id: db_sensitivity_sweep, tau_schedule_sweep, training_steps_sweep
116	
117	
118	\subsection{Sparsity Scaling and Regime Analysis}
119	\label{sec:scaling}
120	
121	Table~\ref{tab:scaling} and Figure~\ref{fig:sparsity_sweep} show PPL as a function of sparsity for the KL predictor under global allocation and vanilla TEAL.
122	
123	\begin{figure}[t]
124	\centering
125	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig2_sparsity_sweep.pdf}
126	\caption{Perplexity scaling with sparsity. The KL predictor's advantage grows disproportionately as more neurons are pruned.}
127	\label{fig:sparsity_sweep}
128	\end{figure}
129	
130	\begin{table}[t]
131	\centering
132	\caption{PPL scaling with sparsity (WikiText-2). KL advantage grows disproportionately with sparsity.}
133	\label{tab:scaling}
134	\small
135	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
136	\toprule
137	Sparsity & KL (Ours) & TEAL vanilla & Relative advantage \\
138	\midrule
139	30\% & \textbf{8.98} & 10.97 & 18\% \\ % exp_id: kl_30_global_teal
140	50\% & \textbf{11.79} & 23.31 & 49\% \\ % exp_id: bench_kl50_global
141	70\% & \textbf{17.91} & 100.11 & 82\% \\ % exp_id: kl_70_global_teal
142	\bottomrule
143	\end{tabular}
144	\end{table}
145	
146	The KL advantage grows from 18\% at 30\% to 82\% at 70\%, where TEAL collapses (PPL 100.11) while the learned predictor maintains coherent allocation.
147	In absolute terms, KL/Dense degradation is $1.47\times$ at 30\%, $1.93\times$ at 50\%, and $2.93\times$ at 70\%, compared to TEAL/Dense ratios of $1.79\times$, $3.81\times$, and $16.4\times$ respectively.
148	
149	\paragraph{Three Operating Regions.}
150	Table~\ref{tab:phase} presents global vs.\ uniform allocation at three sparsity levels, revealing qualitative shifts in allocation preference. Denser sampling (e.g., 35\% sparsity) would be needed to precisely locate region boundaries.
151	
152	\begin{table}[t]
153	\centering
154	\caption{Allocation analysis: global (TEAL) vs.\ uniform per-layer allocation across sparsity levels. 30\% and 50\% KL rows report 3-seed mean$\pm$std for MMLU; other metrics use seed 42. Each row uses a predictor trained at the respective sparsity target.}
155	\label{tab:phase}
156	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
157	\begin{tabular}{llccccc}
158	\toprule
159	Sparsity & Allocation & PPL$\downarrow$ & ARC-c & WG & MMLU & GSM8K \\
160	\midrule
161	0\% & Dense & 6.12 & 58.28 & 78.06 & 65.27 & 48.75 \\
162	\midrule
163	\multirow{3}{*}{30\%}
164	& TEAL vanilla & 10.97 & \textbf{42.32} & 66.06 & 38.61 & 7.88 \\ % exp_id: bench_teal30
165	& KL global & 8.98 & 39.68 & \textbf{70.17} & 35.7$\pm$9.5 & \textbf{8.79} \\ % exp_id: kl30_3seed_global
166	& KL uniform & \textbf{8.82} & 40.78 & 68.59 & \textbf{40.7$\pm$1.3} & 7.35 \\ % exp_id: kl30_3seed_uniform
167	\midrule
168	\multirow{2}{*}{40\%}
169	& KL global & 10.12 & 40.96 & 65.35 & \textbf{38.06} & \textbf{5.00} \\ % exp_id: bench_kl40_global
170	& KL uniform & \textbf{8.36} & \textbf{41.81} & \textbf{67.17} & 30.68 & 3.94 \\ % exp_id: d030_kl40_uniform
171	\midrule
172	\multirow{3}{*}{50\%}
173	& TEAL vanilla & 23.31 & 28.41 & 53.04 & \textbf{28.32} & 1.97 \\ % exp_id: bench_teal50
174	& KL global & \textbf{11.79} & \textbf{32.85} & \textbf{63.46} & 28.1$\pm$0.2 & 1.29 \\ % exp_id: multi_seed_kl50_global
175	& KL uniform & 11.96 & 32.76 & 62.90 & 28.0$\pm$0.6 & \textbf{2.12} \\ % exp_id: multi_seed_kl50_uniform
176	\bottomrule
177	\end{tabular}}
178	\end{table}
179	
180	The allocation preference is \emph{non-monotonic}. We observe three qualitative behaviors at the sampled sparsity levels (7--8B scale):
181	
182	\noindent\textbf{Budget-surplus ($\leq$30\%).}
183	Uniform allocation provides $7.5\times$ smaller cross-seed MMLU standard deviation ($\sigma$: 1.3pp vs.\ 9.5pp), eliminating catastrophic seed-dependent degradation under global top-$k$ (MMLU 35.7$\pm$9.5\% vs.\ 40.7$\pm$1.3\%, 3-seed). Global top-$k$ starves late layers (L31: 28.4\%, std/mean$=$1.89), and this starvation interacts unpredictably with predictor initialization (Appendix~\ref{app:lagrangian}). % exp_id: kl30_3seed
184	
185	\noindent\textbf{Budget-constrained ($\sim$40\%).}
186	The preference reverses: global achieves MMLU 38.06\% vs.\ uniform's 30.68\% (+7.4pp). % exp_id: bench_kl40_global, d030_kl40_uniform
187	PPL remains low (8.36) but downstream accuracy degrades, confirming PPL is a poor proxy for reasoning.
188	
189	\noindent\textbf{Capacity-limited ($\geq$50\%).}
190	Global/uniform gap vanishes (MMLU 28.1$\pm$0.2\% vs.\ 28.0$\pm$0.6\%, $\sigma\leq$0.6pp; contrast 9.5pp at 30\%), confirming capacity limitation. % exp_id: multi_seed_kl50_global, multi_seed_kl50_uniform
191	Late-layer starvation persists across levels (L24--31 retention: 50.1/34.2/22.6\% at 30/50/70\% sparsity; Figure~\ref{fig:retention}), consistent on both 7--8B models (\S\ref{sec:cross_arch}).
192	
193	\paragraph{Gap Decomposition.}
194	Decomposing the Dense$\to$KL gap under uniform allocation (5.85 PPL): per-token hard mask evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:db_sensitivity}) yields PPL 9.22, attributing 53\% to predictor approximation (including discretization) and 47\% to per-layer budget allocation.
195	Even under global allocation, the learned predictor remains $1.98\times$ better than TEAL (11.79 vs.\ 23.31).
196	
197	
198	\subsection{SPON Orthogonality Analysis}
199	\label{sec:spon}
200	
201	At 50\% sparsity, the predictor's hidden-state perturbation (L2=482.65) and SPON's additive correction (L2=76.2, cosine similarity 0.196) are weakly correlated ($R^2$=0.038); SPON yields only 2.4\% PPL improvement (12.08$\to$11.79), confirming the KL predictor already captures most recoverable signal. % exp_id: spon_decomposition, spon_2048_s42, mvp_kl_norm_v2_s42
202	
203	\paragraph{Cross-Architecture Validation.}
204	\label{sec:cross_arch}
205	Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch} evaluates on Mistral-7B-v0.3~\cite{jiang2023mistral} (GQA + sliding window, dense PPL 5.52).
206	
207	\begin{table}[t]
208	\centering
209	\caption{Cross-architecture comparison (WikiText-2 PPL$\downarrow$). Adv = TEAL\,/\,KL ratio. LLaMA uses global top-$k$; Mistral uses uniform allocation (matched within each architecture).}
210	\label{tab:cross_arch}
211	\small
212	\begin{tabular}{l@{\hspace{4pt}}cc@{\hspace{3pt}}c@{\hspace{6pt}}|@{\hspace{6pt}}cc@{\hspace{3pt}}c}
213	\toprule
214	 & \multicolumn{3}{c}{Mistral-7B} & \multicolumn{3}{c}{LLaMA-8B} \\
215	 & KL & TEAL & Adv & KL & TEAL & Adv \\
216	\midrule

1	\appendix
2	
3	\section{Inference Efficiency}
4	\label{app:latency}
5	
6	Table~\ref{tab:latency} reports inference throughput on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (batch size 1, sequence length 2048, fp16, averaged over 100 forward passes).
7	
8	\begin{table}[h]
9	\centering
10	\caption{Inference latency on LLaMA-3.1-8B (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, batch=1, seq=2048, fp16, 100 forward passes). Overhead is relative to dense inference.}
11	\label{tab:latency}
12	\small
13	\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
14	\toprule
15	Method & Sparsity & ms/fwd & tok/s & Overhead \\
16	\midrule
17	Dense & 0\% & 119.11$\pm$0.57 & 17{,}195 & --- \\
18	\midrule
19	KL predictor-only & 30\% & 126.64$\pm$0.70 & 16{,}172 & +6.3\% \\ % exp_id: latency_bench
20	KL predictor-only & 50\% & 126.78$\pm$0.31 & 16{,}154 & +6.4\% \\ % exp_id: latency_bench
21	\midrule
22	Predictor + compensation & 30\% & 129.94$\pm$0.75 & 15{,}761 & +9.1\% \\ % exp_id: latency_bench
23	Predictor + compensation & 50\% & 129.71$\pm$0.53 & 15{,}789 & +8.9\% \\ % exp_id: latency_bench
24	\bottomrule
25	\end{tabular}
26	\end{table}
27	
28	The full KL-sparse pipeline adds 6.4\% overhead to dense inference (126.78 vs.\ 119.11\,ms/forward), of which the predictor's 32-layer forward pass contributes 3.17\,ms (2.7\%); the remainder arises from mask application and sparse FFN indexing.
29	Eliminating the compensation network saves an additional $\sim$2.7\% latency overhead and 67.2M parameters (the per-layer GEMV required for output rescaling), confirming that KL distillation provides both quality and efficiency advantages over BCE-based approaches.
30	The overhead is near-identical at 30\% and 50\% sparsity because the predictor runs the same computation regardless of target sparsity; only the top-$k$ threshold changes.
31	
32	Note that the current implementation uses unstructured element-wise masks, which do not translate to wall-clock speedup without sparse kernel support.
33	The pipeline adds $\sim$6.4\% overhead; net acceleration requires kernel-level sparse computation optimizations (e.g., Triton block-sparse, cuSPARSE) that are beyond the scope of this work.
34	Our contribution is prediction quality and inference simplification (removing the compensation network), not end-to-end latency reduction.
35	
36	
37	\section{Predictor Bottleneck Sensitivity}
38	\label{app:db_sensitivity}
39	
40	Table~\ref{tab:db_sensitivity} reports the effect of predictor bottleneck dimension $d_b$ on PPL at 50\% sparsity under both TEAL global allocation (the paper's primary inference protocol) and per-token evaluation.
41	
42	\begin{table}[h]
43	\centering
44	\caption{Predictor bottleneck sensitivity at 50\% sparsity (WikiText-2 PPL$\downarrow$). TEAL global is the primary inference protocol; per-token shown for reference.}
45	\label{tab:db_sensitivity}
46	\small
47	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
48	\toprule
49	$d_b$ & Params & TEAL global & $\Delta$ & Per-token \\
50	\midrule
51	64 & 38.2M (0.48\%) & 12.076 & +0.9\% & 10.16 \\ % exp_id: db_sensitivity_sweep
52	128 & 75.9M (0.95\%) & 11.963 & --- & 9.218 \\ % exp_id: db_sensitivity_sweep
53	256 & 151.5M (1.89\%) & 12.105 & +1.2\% & 8.586 \\ % exp_id: db_sensitivity_sweep
54	512 & 302.5M (3.77\%) & 12.315 & +2.9\% & 7.93 \\ % exp_id: db_sensitivity_sweep
55	\bottomrule
56	\end{tabular}
57	\end{table}
58	
59	Under TEAL global allocation, increasing $d_b$ beyond 128 provides no benefit (PPL slightly worsens), while per-token evaluation shows monotonic improvement (10.16$\to$7.93).
60	This divergence indicates that the global top-$k$ allocation mechanism, not predictor capacity, is the binding constraint: additional predictor capacity produces better per-neuron scores, but the global ranking and budget distribution cannot exploit them.
61	The $d_b{=}128$ configuration (75.9M params, $<$1\% of base model) is therefore optimal for the TEAL inference protocol.
62	
63	\subsection{Temperature Schedule Sensitivity}
64	\label{app:tau_sensitivity}
65	
66	\begin{table}[h]
67	\centering
68	\caption{Temperature schedule sensitivity at 50\% sparsity (WikiText-2 PPL$\downarrow$, TEAL global).}
69	\label{tab:tau_sensitivity}
70	\small
71	\begin{tabular}{lc}
72	\toprule
73	$\tau$ Schedule & PPL$\downarrow$ \\
74	\midrule
75	Fixed $\tau{=}0.5$ & \textbf{11.861} \\ % exp_id: tau_schedule_sweep
76	Linear $1.0 \to 0.1$ (default) & 11.963 \\ % exp_id: tau_schedule_sweep
77	Fixed $\tau{=}0.1$ & 12.072 \\ % exp_id: tau_schedule_sweep
78	\bottomrule
79	\end{tabular}
80	\end{table}
81	
82	Temperature schedule has minimal impact ($<$1.8\% PPL variation).
83	The linear annealing default is a conservative choice; even removing annealing entirely (fixed $\tau{=}0.5$) yields comparable performance.
84	
85	\subsection{Training Convergence}
86	\label{app:training_convergence}
87	
88	\begin{table}[h]
89	\centering
90	\caption{Training convergence at 50\% sparsity (WikiText-2 PPL$\downarrow$, TEAL global).}
91	\label{tab:training_convergence}
92	\small
93	\begin{tabular}{cc}
94	\toprule
95	Steps & PPL$\downarrow$ \\
96	\midrule
97	200 & 15.158 \\ % exp_id: training_steps_sweep
98	400 & 12.538 \\ % exp_id: training_steps_sweep

100	800 & 11.907 \\ % exp_id: training_steps_sweep

102	\bottomrule
103	\end{tabular}
104	\end{table}
105	
106	Training converges rapidly: 95\% of the quality gap closes by step 600, and performance saturates by step 800 ($\Delta < 0.001$ between 800 and 1000 steps).
107	Our default of 1000 steps provides a conservative margin.
108	
109	
110	\section{Adaptive Penalty Controller Dynamics}
111	\label{app:lagrangian}
112	
113	Table~\ref{tab:lagrangian} reports the convergence of the adaptive penalty controller across sparsity targets.
114	The geometric doubling pattern ($1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 8 \to \ldots$) enables $\lambda$ to reach steady state within $\sim$10 steps; the deadzone ($\epsilon = 0.02$) then stabilizes $\lambda$ once actual sparsity is within $\pm$2\% of the target.
115	
116	\begin{table}[h]
117	\centering
118	\caption{Penalty controller convergence across sparsity targets (multiplicative schedule, margin $\epsilon=0.02$, 1000 training steps). Deviation is $|$actual $-$ target$|$ / target.}
119	\label{tab:lagrangian}
120	\small
121	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
122	\toprule
123	Target $\rho$ & $\lambda_{\max}$ & Final $\lambda$ & Actual sparsity & Deviation \\
124	\midrule
125	30\% & 5000 & 5000 (cap) & 0.285 & 5.0\% \\ % exp_id: kl_30pct_s42
126	40\% & 5000 & 625 & 0.398 & 0.5\% \\ % exp_id: kl_40pct_s42
127	50\% & 1000 & 8 & 0.504 & 0.8\% \\ % exp_id: kl_50pct_s42
128	70\% & 1000 & 1000 (cap) & 0.688 & 1.7\% \\ % exp_id: kl_70pct_s42
129	\bottomrule
130	\end{tabular}
131	\end{table}
132	
133	At 50\% sparsity, the SwiGLU gate distribution already clusters near the target, so $\lambda$ remains low (8); the constraint is nearly satisfied by the initial predictor outputs.
134	At 30\% and 70\%, the gap between the gate prior and target is larger, driving $\lambda$ to its respective caps.
135	The 40\% target converges to $\lambda = 625$ with only 0.5\% deviation, illustrating the controller's precision when the target is reachable without saturating.
136	
137	\begin{figure}[h]
138	\centering
139	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{lagrangian_dynamics.pdf}
140	\caption{Adaptive penalty controller convergence across sparsity targets. Upper panel: penalty weight $\lambda$ (log scale) over training steps. The 30\% target requires extreme penalty ($\lambda \to 5000$) to suppress activations below their natural density, while 50\% needs only $\lambda \approx 8$ since SwiGLU gates already cluster near this sparsity. Lower panel: actual sparsity (solid) converges to the target (dashed) within $\sim$10 steps via geometric doubling.}
141	\label{fig:lagrangian_dynamics}
142	\end{figure}
143	
144	Temperature $\tau$ is annealed linearly from 1.0 to 0.1 over 1000 steps.
145	A mild loss increase in the final $\sim$100 steps is expected: as masks become more binary ($\tau \to 0$), discrete rounding noise slightly increases KL divergence, confirming the training is converging toward the hard-mask inference regime.
146	
147	The controller reliably drives actual sparsity to within 5\% of the target across all tested regimes, with $\lambda$ spanning three orders of magnitude (8 to 5000) via geometric doubling.
148	
149	
150	\section{Out-of-Distribution Evaluation}
151	\label{app:ood}
152	
153	To address concerns about data homogeneity between training (WikiText-103) and evaluation (WikiText-2), we evaluate on C4~\cite{raffel2020c4} validation set at 50\% sparsity under TEAL global allocation.
154	
155	\begin{table}[h]
156	\centering
157	\caption{Out-of-distribution evaluation on C4 validation (50\% sparsity, PPL$\downarrow$).}
158	\label{tab:ood}
159	\small
160	\begin{tabular}{lc}
161	\toprule
162	Method & C4 PPL$\downarrow$ \\
163	\midrule
164	Dense & 9.21 \\
165	KL predictor (Ours) & \textbf{18.40} \\ % exp_id: eval_c4_ood_kl50
166	TEAL vanilla & 38.75 \\
167	\bottomrule
168	\end{tabular}
169	\end{table}
170	
171	The KL-trained predictor achieves 52.5\% relative advantage over TEAL on out-of-domain data (18.40 vs.\ 38.75), comparable to or slightly exceeding the 49\% advantage observed on WikiText-2 (11.79 vs.\ 23.31), suggesting that KL-trained predictions generalize to held-out data when the evaluation distribution differs from training.
172	This confirms that the predictor learns generalizable neuron importance patterns rather than overfitting to the WikiText training distribution.
173	
174	
175	\section{Per-Layer Retention Analysis}
176	\label{app:retention}
177	
178	\begin{figure}[h]
179	\centering
180	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{per_layer_retention_chart.pdf}
181	\caption{Per-layer neuron retention under global top-$k$ allocation at 30\%, 50\%, and 70\% sparsity. Dashed lines indicate uniform retention baselines. Late layers (L24--31) are consistently starved due to long-tailed activation distributions, with retention dropping to 28.4\% (L31) even at 30\% sparsity. At 70\%, starvation extends to mid-layers (L10--12: 16.7--20.1\%), explaining the transition to the capacity-limited regime.}
182	\label{fig:retention}
183	\end{figure}
184	
185	
186	\section{Training Stability}
187	\label{app:stability}
188	
189	Three-seed evaluation ($s \in \{42, 123, 456\}$) at 50\% sparsity under uniform allocation yields PPL $11.92 \pm 0.07$ (CV=0.6\%), confirming training stability across random initializations. % exp_id: multi_seed_kl50_uniform
190	Downstream metrics are similarly stable: ARC-c $33.8 \pm 1.2$\%, WinoGrande $62.9 \pm 0.1$\%, MMLU $28.0 \pm 0.6$\%, GSM8K $2.2 \pm 0.1$\%.
191	
192	Under global allocation at 50\%, MMLU is equally stable: $28.1 \pm 0.2$\% (s42=27.89, s123=28.34, s456=27.94), confirming that the near-random performance is capacity-limited rather than seed-sensitive ($\sigma$=0.2pp vs.\ 9.5pp at 30\% global). % exp_id: multi_seed_kl50_global
193	The low standard deviation across both allocation strategies indicates that the KL training landscape is well-conditioned for this predictor architecture, with low sensitivity to initialization.

Now I'm looking at the results for Qwen-2.5-14B to show how the KL predictor generalizes to larger models—it maintains a consistent advantage ratio around 1.15x over TEAL, similar to what we see at smaller scales, though the BCE predictor completely fails on this architecture due to training collapse. the cross-architecture table as is, since adding Qwen with incomplete data would disrupt the visual consistency.

Now I'm checking the oracle F1 data to see if anything needs updating there.

Looking at the precision and recall metrics, BCE achieves much better balance with 0.613 F1 compared to KL's 0.540, despite KL having worse perplexity by a significant margin. The key insight is that KL's low precision around 0.51 shows it's optimizing for distributional properties rather than actually matching magnitudes well, which explains why it fails at the oracle task even though both use identical architectures and allocation strategies. I'm checking the existing Qwen-14B references in the paper to see what experiments are already documented and which ones are still running.

28	At 30\% sparsity, KL distillation with global TEAL allocation achieves PPL 8.98, reducing TEAL's degradation from dense (10.97 $\to$ 8.98, an 18\% improvement). % exp_id: kl_30_global_teal

196	\section{Extended Downstream Evaluation}
197	\label{app:downstream}
198	
199	Table~\ref{tab:downstream} compares Dense, KL 30\% (uniform allocation), and TEAL 30\% on three additional downstream benchmarks not included in the main results.
200	
201	\begin{table}[h]
202	\centering
203	\caption{Extended downstream benchmarks at 30\% sparsity (LLaMA-3.1-8B, seed 42). HellaSwag: 10-shot normalized acc; PIQA: 0-shot normalized acc; BoolQ: 0-shot acc.}
204	\label{tab:downstream}
205	\small
206	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
207	\toprule
208	Method & HellaSwag & PIQA & BoolQ \\
209	\midrule
210	Dense & \textbf{82.33} & \textbf{80.74} & \textbf{82.94} \\
211	KL 30\% uniform & 72.70 & 75.95 & 76.85 \\ % exp_id: downstream_extended_kl30_s42
212	TEAL 30\% vanilla & 66.70 & 73.61 & 68.50 \\ % exp_id: downstream_teal30_baseline
213	\bottomrule
214	\end{tabular}
215	\end{table}
216	
217	The KL predictor outperforms TEAL on all three benchmarks. On HellaSwag, it preserves 88.3\% of dense accuracy (72.70 vs.\ 82.33) vs.\ 81.0\% for TEAL (66.70). BoolQ shows the largest gap: 92.7\% vs.\ 82.6\% preservation. PIQA shows a smaller differential (94.1\% vs.\ 91.2\%).
218

224	
225	The KL advantage ratio (computed within each architecture under matched allocation) is consistent across architectures (within 8\% at $\leq$50\% sparsity), with larger variance at 70\% (4.63$\times$ vs.\ 5.59$\times$) due to differential baseline collapse.
226	Consistent ratios despite Mistral's stronger TEAL baseline (gate distribution favors magnitude pruning) provide preliminary evidence of generality across SwiGLU architectures at the 7--8B scale.
227	
228	\paragraph{Scale Generalization: Qwen-2.5-14B.}
229	On Qwen-2.5-14B~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} (dense PPL 5.18), KL distillation at 30\% sparsity achieves PPL 7.62 ($1.47\times$ dense) vs.\ TEAL vanilla PPL 8.76 ($1.69\times$), a $1.15\times$ advantage consistent with the 7--8B results (LLaMA: $1.22\times$, Mistral: $1.24\times$). % exp_id: qwen14b_kl30_s42
230	BCE training fails on this architecture: the predictor collapses to 6.4\% native sparsity within 50 steps, with no recovery over the remaining 950 steps. % exp_id: qwen14b_bce30_s42
231	A $10\times$ stronger penalty ($\lambda_{\max}{=}50{,}000$) produces identical collapse, confirming that BCE gradient insufficiency (\S\ref{sec:method:gradient}) is architecture-general. % exp_id: qwen14b_bce30_s42_v2
232	
233	
234	\paragraph{Inference Efficiency.}
235	The pipeline adds 6.4\% overhead to dense inference (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) while removing the compensation network ($-$2.7\% latency, $-$67.2M params); post-hoc SPON yields $<$3\% additional gain (\S\ref{sec:spon}), suggesting the predictor already internalizes most error-correction signal (Appendix~\ref{app:latency}).
236	
237	\paragraph{Training Stability.}
238	Three-seed evaluation (50\%): PPL $11.92 \pm 0.07$, MMLU $\sigma\leq$0.6pp (Appendix~\ref{app:stability}).
